evidence.quote: Samples were prepared by spin-coating a solution containing 0.25 mM titanium (IV) isopropoxide in ethanol onto 3 mm thick FTO (sheet resistance 7Ω/, Ra 12 nm) glass. The substrate was heated at 500°C to sinter the c-TiO2 leaving a 50 nm layer. A mixed halide (CH3NH3PbI3 -xClx) perovskite precursor was prepared in DMF with a 5 wt% Al2O3 nanoparticle addition as described elsewhere.10 The precursor was deposited in a single process onto the glass using spin-coating and was annealed under various NIR intensities and durations to give a film thickness of between 450-500 nm.

Samples were annealed at lamp power levels ranging from 55% to 85% at 5% increments. At each level, sample exposure time was gradually decreased by iteratively increasing the conveyor speed by 0.5 m/minute; the total length of the NIR active region was 0.4 m. Samples were characterised by extracting RGB (red, green, blue) colour values from images taken of the samples under a calibrated light source. Fig. 3 demonstrates a series of samples imaged under the consistent light. Once annealed, a solution containing spiro-OMeTAD and additives (tBP and Li-TFSI) was deposited (200 nm) onto the annealed perovskite layer and capped with a gold contact evaporated at 10⁻4 torr.

At maximum power the lamps have a power density of 250 kW m-2. The lamp to sample separation is maintained at 10 cm throughout the experiment. In this work, we present an alternative method of postannealing perovskite films which reduces the time required to as little as 2.5 seconds whilst maintaining high PCEs. This was achieved by exposing the freshly deposited perovskite film to a short burst of near-infrared (NIR) radiation using commercially available NIR lamps. The NIR region of the electromagnetic spectrum is situated between the visible and the infrared with wavelengths ranging from 700 nm to 2500 nm, peaking at 1000 nm. NIR sintering of porous TiO 2 films has already been demonstrated for use in DSCs 21,22 and much like the TiO 2 precusor paste used to make DSCs the perovskite precursor

The NIR equipment (Adphos Coil Lab LV2, tungsten filament halogen lamps) has an output spectrum in the region of 250 - 2500nm, peaking between 800 and 1200 nm as can be seen in Fig 1 as well as elsewhere24,25. At maximum power the lamps have a power density of 250 kW m-2. The lamp to sample separation is maintained at 10 cm throughout the experiment. The NIR output was controlled by varying the percentage lamp power and the duration for which samples were exposed to the radiation was controlled by varying the speed of a conveyor system passing beneath the lamp.

Once a trend between optimal NIR parameters and sample homogeneity had been established, full devices were fabricated using the NIR oven to anneal the perovskite light absorber at different speeds. NIR lamp power was fixed at 85% for this investigation, a power density approximately equal to 50 W cm-2. In addition, oven annealed devices were also made. The results of an analysis of the JV data produced is seen in Fig. 4. Overall the oven annealed devices show higher PCEs compared to NIR counterparts owing to increased Voc and fill factor. However, Jsc appeared consistently higher in the NIR samples compared to the oven annealed counterparts.

A rapid annealing technique for CH 3 NH3 PbI 3 perovskite solar cells is presented. We report a co-deposited Al 2 O3 perovskite device annealed in under 2.5 seconds with a PCE of 10.0% compared to 10.9% for a 45 minute ovenannealed device.

population_statistics.label: Statistical analysis of JV data for devices annealed under different NIR exposure times and oven-annealed comparison devices

evidence.quote: Once a trend between optimal NIR parameters and sample homogeneity had been established, full devices were fabricated using the NIR oven to anneal the perovskite light absorber at different speeds. NIR lamp power was fixed at 85% for this investigation, a power density approximately equal to 50 W cm-2. In addition, oven annealed devices were also made. The results of an analysis of the JV data produced is seen in Fig. 4. Overall the oven annealed devices show higher PCEs compared to NIR counterparts owing to increased Voc and fill factor. However, Jsc appeared consistently higher in the NIR samples compared to the oven annealed counterparts.

metrics.name: reported photovoltaic impact of preferential orientation
metrics.raw_value: does not seem to impact on the photovoltaic performance of the devices

evidence.quote: The high intensity of the peaks at 14.04° and 28.38° associated to the (110) and (220) crystal planes, relatively to other characteristic peaks of the CH3NH3PbI3, labelled as (112), (211), (202), (114) and (134) is indicative of the growth of large crystals with preferential orientation such as the (110) and (220) plane are oriented parallel to the substrate. The subfigure in Fig 7, where the XRD spectra have been normalised to the (110) peak shows that the preferential orientation of the CH3NH3PbI3 crystal lattice is more pronounced in the case of NIR annealed compared to oven annealed films. However, this observation does not seem to impact on the photovoltaic performance of the devices.

Once a trend between optimal NIR parameters and sample homogeneity had been established, full devices were fabricated using the NIR oven to anneal the perovskite light absorber at different speeds. NIR lamp power was fixed at 85% for this investigation, a power density approximately equal to 50 W cm-2. In addition, oven annealed devices were also made. The results of an analysis of the JV data produced is seen in Fig. 4. Overall the oven annealed devices show higher PCEs compared to NIR counterparts owing to increased Voc and fill factor. However, Jsc appeared consistently higher in the NIR samples compared to the oven annealed counterparts.

It can also be seen that whilst short-circuit current appears to be consistent with different exposure times, open-circuit voltage and fill factor are more sensitive to change. Voc o r o na adr ar 2.47 s, after which a decrease is seen on account of resistive losses caused by incomplete crystallisation and solvent removal. Pockets of trapped solvent at the perovskite-spiro interface may also be thought to induce recombination losses, hence the lower fill factor. Fig.4 illustrates that small fluctuations in annealingtime can lead to changes in PCE. In upscalingthis can be addressed by optimisation and expansion of the process window.

The high intensity of the peaks at 14.04° and 28.38° associated to the (110) and (220) crystal planes, relatively to other characteristic peaks of the CH3NH3PbI3, labelled as (112), (211), (202), (114) and (134) is indicative of the growth of large crystals with preferential orientation such as the (110) and (220) plane are oriented parallel to the substrate. The subfigure in Fig 7, where the XRD spectra have been normalised to the (110) peak shows that the preferential orientation of the CH3NH3PbI3 crystal lattice is more pronounced in the case of NIR annealed compared to oven annealed films. However, this observation does not seem to impact on the photovoltaic performance of the devices.

unresolved_notes: The Experimental section identifies the absorber precursor as “mixed halide (CH3NH3PbI3 -xClx) perovskite precursor,” whereas the abstract and XRD discussion use CH3NH3PbI3 wording. The evidence does not establish separate complete-device designs, so these descriptions are retained within one family rather than split into separate families.
NIR and oven annealing are mutually exclusive processing arms for the same reported finished-device architecture and therefore do not define separate device families.

The abstract-reported devices with PCEs of 10.0% and 10.9% are not explicitly identified as the same physical specimens as the later Fig. 5 “highest performing” devices. They are therefore retained as separate individual devices and observations rather than linked by inference.
The source does not explicitly report the device polarity. Although the ordered layers could suggest a conventional topology, polarity is left not reported rather than inferred.

The 55% to 85% lamp-power range, 5% increments, 0.5 m/minute conveyor-speed increments, and 0.4 m active-region length describe the NIR sample-optimization procedure. The evidence does not establish them as properties of every complete device or of a particular measured device, so they are not propagated to the device family or individual devices.

The approximately 200°C FTO temperature was measured for a 2.47 s exposed sample, but the evidence does not establish that this thermal-imaging sample was a complete photovoltaic device or any reported performance device; it is therefore excluded from individual-device and performance records.

The film samples used for colour analysis, SEM, XRD, and precursor absorbance measurements are characterization specimens rather than complete photovoltaic devices and are excluded from device-family, individual-device, performance, population, and stability records.
The supplied evidence reports no device-aging or operational-stability outcome.
The supplied evidence does not report a complete ordered photovoltaic stack or polarity, so no device family can be safely created for the rapidly annealed cells.

The conclusion's statement that solar cells were produced with "PCEs over 10%" is a broad study-level claim without an identified individual device, sample size, or explicit population statistic; it is therefore not represented as a device or population record.

The fixed 85% NIR lamp power, approximate power density, and different annealing speeds describe device groups rather than identified specimens, so they cannot safely be assigned as IndividualDevice properties.
